title: Agents & Claude Code
scopeHtml: Scope: workflow vs agent, the three wiring paths, human-in-the-loop placement, Claude Code permission modes and settings, CLAUDE.md, rules, hooks, subagents and plugins.

questions.promptHtml:
A task always follows the same five steps and inputs are well constrained. What should you build?

  • A. An agent, for flexibility
  • B. A workflow, because you can enumerate the steps in code
  • C. A multi-agent orchestrator
  • D. Nothing; it cannot be automated

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Start with the simplest pattern: single call, then workflow, then agent only if the path cannot be enumerated.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Agents add behavioral complexity and transcript-level observability needs. Choose an agent when you can specify the goal and tools but not the path, and inputs vary unpredictably.

questions.promptHtml:
A healthcare product handles PHI and needs a long-running agent. A teammate suggests Claude Managed Agents because it removes the loop and sandbox work. What is the problem?

  • A. Managed Agents cannot call tools
  • B. Managed Agent sessions are stateful and stored server-side, so they are not currently eligible for Zero Data Retention or a HIPAA BAA; use the Agent SDK or a raw loop on a covered configuration
  • C. Managed Agents only run for seconds
  • D. There is no problem; BAAs cover beta features

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. The governing compliance constraint picks the wiring path before convenience does.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Three paths: raw Messages API loop (you own everything), Agent SDK (runs the loop in your process; you still execute tools), Managed Agents (public beta; Anthropic runs the loop and sandbox; agent defined as a versioned API resource; beta header managed-agents-2026-04-01). A BAA also excludes Console, Workbench, beta features and consumer plans.

questions.contextHtml: A config-editing agent (read_file, write_file, validate_config) was tested in a scratch directory. In a customer environment it corrected an out-of-range rate limit, validate_config passed, the loop exited. Minutes later the customer's app was throttled and failing.
questions.promptHtml:
What design step was missing?

  • A. More loop iterations
  • B. A checkpoint between "proposed change ready" and "write committed", placed by asking the worst outcome if write_file runs unchecked
  • C. A stricter schema for validate_config
  • D. Lower temperature

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blaming the validator or the loop cap.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What depends on that value downstream? Is the environment reversible?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restore the old value.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Missing HITL gate; validator too narrow; exit condition too narrow.
  4. How I'd verify each: Review the exit condition and the tool's blast radius.
  5. Root cause: Exit condition scoped to the file; no gate before a production write.
  6. Fix: Pause and surface proposed changes for human approval before the first live write (or a PreToolUse hook); keep a dry-run mode.
  7. Prevention: Ask the worst-case question during tool scoping, not after the first incident.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not gate every read; reserve gates for irreversible actions.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Other insertion points? → After a planning step (wrong plan), and on unexpected output (error, empty, out-of-bounds).

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes the loop.
  • Hire: adds approval.
  • Strong hire: places gates by worst-case cost and enforces with a hook.

questions.promptHtml:
Which mode is built for locked-down CI where anything not pre-approved must be refused with no prompt queue?

  • A. acceptEdits
  • B. plan
  • C. dontAsk
  • D. bypassPermissions

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: C. dontAsk auto-approves only allow-listed tools plus read-only commands and auto-denies the rest.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: default prompts on edits and commands; acceptEdits allows edits and common filesystem commands (mkdir touch rm rmdir mv cp sed) inside the working directory; plan blocks edits and commands until a plan is approved; auto lets a classifier review each action and blocks risky ones (research preview); bypassPermissions skips all prompts and the protected-path guard and is only for disposable containers or VMs.

questions.contextHtml: A developer switched to bypassPermissions to rename /v1/legacy/ endpoint references. A cleanup script matched the same pattern in /deploy/config/prod/ and deleted three files with no prompt.
questions.promptHtml:
What should have been done?

  • A. Nothing; this was unforeseeable
  • B. Set deny rules on sensitive directories first, and use auto (classifier-gated) or default/acceptEdits instead of a full bypass
  • C. Trust the agent more
  • D. Run the script in plan mode

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Treating it as a model bug instead of a configuration choice.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the pattern anchored to /src/? Was an enterprise deny rule set?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restore from version control or backups.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Over-broad glob; no deny rule; bypass mode.
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay the match in a dry run.
  5. Root cause: Over-broad pattern plus a mode with no checkpoints.
  6. Fix: B. Note the gate would have been the script invocation prompt in default mode.
  7. Prevention: Enterprise deny rule on /deploy/config/**; deny always beats allow.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not use bypass on a workstation against a live codebase.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html: • Would acceptEdits have stopped direct rm in the working dir? → No, it auto-approves rm inside the working directory.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the agent.
  • Hire: sets deny rules.
  • Strong hire: explains where the gate sat and chooses auto plus enterprise deny.

questions.promptHtml:
An administrator needs a rule denying edits to .env files that no developer or project file can override. Where does it go?

  • A. ~/.claude/settings.json
  • B. .claude/settings.json in the repo
  • C. .claude/settings.local.json
  • D. Enterprise managed-settings.json

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: D. Managed settings sit above user and project scope and cannot be overridden; deny beats allow in every mode.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Scope order is user, project, local project, then enterprise managed settings; managed sits on top and cannot be overridden by users or project files. A deny rule always beats an allow rule regardless of mode, so an enterprise deny is the most durable governance control. User, project and local files are all editable by developers or the repo.

questions.promptHtml:
"Run the formatter after every edit" and "never touch /legacy/tokens/" must hold every single time. How should each be enforced?

  • A. Write both in CLAUDE.md
  • B. A PostToolUse hook for the formatter and a PreToolUse hook (exit code 2) or deny rule for the protected path
  • C. A longer system prompt
  • D. A subagent

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Hooks run independently of the model's decision; CLAUDE.md is a suggestion that dilutes as it grows.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: PreToolUse can block (exit 2, reason on stderr); PostToolUse cannot block, which suits formatters, tests and audit logging. Others: UserPromptSubmit, Stop, Notification, SessionStart, SessionEnd. In an incident an 847-line CLAUDE.md let a one-line path restriction get ignored by dilution; keep CLAUDE.md to behavior-changing rules and path-scope the rest with .claude/rules/ using a paths glob (a rule without paths loads at launch like CLAUDE.md, regardless of folder).

questions.promptHtml:
You delegate a refactor to the built-in Explore subagent expecting it to respect your CLAUDE.md conventions. It does not. Why?

  • A. CLAUDE.md is ignored everywhere
  • B. Explore and Plan skip CLAUDE.md and git status for speed; use the general-purpose subagent or a custom subagent that loads the rules
  • C. Subagents inherit skills automatically
  • D. Subagents share the parent's full history

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Subagents start clean; only the general-purpose one loads CLAUDE.md, and custom ones need skills listed explicitly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Subagents start from a clean slate and do not inherit conversation history or skills (they do inherit the parent's permission context). Explore and Plan skip CLAUDE.md and git status to stay fast and cheap; the general-purpose subagent loads both. For work that must respect project rules, use general-purpose or a custom subagent in .claude/agents that lists the skills and rules it needs.

questions.promptHtml:
A plugin named payments ships a run-tests command. How is it invoked, and what is the portability risk?

  • A. /run-tests; no risk
  • B. /payments:run-tests; hard-coded absolute paths or environment assumptions will work for the author and fail on other machines
  • C. /plugin run-tests; plugins cannot be shared
  • D. /payments/run-tests; plugin names don't matter

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: B. Plugin commands are namespaced by plugin name, so renaming the plugin renames every command.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: A plugin bundles skills, hooks, subagents and MCP servers, distributed through a marketplace (/plugin marketplace add <owner/repo>). Enterprise admins gate sources with a managed allowlist and push one with extraKnownMarketplaces. Skills are now the recommended format; disable-model-invocation: true makes a skill explicit-only; .claude/commands/ is legacy.
